monitor-roundup.title: The best 27-inch 4K USB-C monitors right now
monitor-roundup.dek: One cable, one panel, and a surprising amount of disagreement about what counts as a stand.
body: The 27-inch 4K USB-C monitor has quietly become the default desk object for anyone who carries a laptop between two places. The pitch is simple: one cable carries video, data and enough power to charge the machine, so docking is a physical act rather than a software one.

We tested nine panels over six weeks. The short version: the differences that matter are the stand, the power budget and the firmware, in that order. Panel quality at this size and resolution has converged to the point where a blind comparison is mostly a comparison of coatings.

Power is where the specification sheets lie by omission. A monitor advertising 90W will often deliver it only when nothing is plugged into its downstream USB ports, which is the exact configuration nobody uses. Two of the nine dropped to 60W with a single external drive attached, which is enough to charge a laptop slower than it discharges.

Our pick is boring and costs $429.99, which is roughly the price at which this category stops feeling like a luxury. Buy the version with the height-adjustable stand even if you think you will not need it.

comments.author: dfarr
comments.text: Nine panels and not one word about matte versus glossy?

devcon-preview.title: DevCon Seattle's schedule is suddenly all about reproducibility
devcon-preview.dek: Three years ago the track did not exist. This year it has its own room.
body: DevCon Seattle published its 2026 schedule this morning, and the reproducibility track has grown from a single lightning-talk slot into a full day with its own room at the Cascade Convention Center.

The keynote sets the tone: a live replay of a distributed failure from a recorded seed, on stage, with the audience allowed to pick the breakpoint. Whether that works in front of 2,000 people is the most interesting engineering question of the conference.
Tickets are still available at http://ticketmaster.com/event/devcon-2026 and the keynote will be streamed at http://youtube.com/watch?v=devcon-keynote

assistants-cite.title: Assistants that show their sources are finally table stakes
assistants-cite.dek: The feature everyone shipped last year is the one everyone is now judged on.
body: An answer without a citation is a rumour with good grammar. That sentence has been on a sticky note in this office for two years, and in 2026 the assistant vendors have finally agreed with it.

The mechanics differ. Some systems retrieve first and generate from what they retrieved; others generate and then go looking for something that agrees. The second approach produces citations that are technically present and practically useless, and users have learned to tell the difference faster than anyone expected.

The test we now apply is embarrassingly simple: click the link. If it resolves to a page that contains the claim, the assistant earned the answer. If it resolves to a plausible-looking homepage, it did not.

comments.author: mkuznetsov
comments.text: "A rumour with good grammar" is going straight into my code review vocabulary.

replay-debugging.title: Replay debugging escapes the lab
replay-debugging.dek: Record-and-replay has been a research toy since the nineties. Three things changed.
body: Record-and-replay debugging is older than most of the engineers using it. The idea - capture a run precisely enough to reproduce it on demand - shows up in research systems going back to the nineties, and it has spent most of that time being too slow, too fragile or too specific to one operating system.

Three things changed. Storage got cheap enough that recording every syscall stopped being absurd. Containerisation made the environment a declared artifact rather than an archaeological question. And a generation of engineers grew up on version control and simply refuses to accept that a failure can be unreproducible.

The result is that replay is now a product category rather than a paper. It is still not free, and the overhead numbers vendors quote are measured on workloads chosen to make them look good. But the argument has shifted from whether it is possible to what you are willing to give up for it.
